articles.title: Which covariance does the single index model keep or omit?
articles.answer: The single index model (SIM) keeps the covariance that comes from shared market exposure. Its diagonal residual approximation omits the covariance between different assets’ residuals, which can make the estimated portfolio risk higher or lower than the sample-covariance result.
articles.body:
The SIM covariance separates a common market contribution from asset-specific residual variances. Its diagonal residual matrix sets the residual covariance between different assets to zero. This is an assumption added on top of fitting each asset by least squares.



**How does the market model supply portfolio inputs?** Assume that the residuals have zero mean, are uncorrelated with market growth, and are uncorrelated across assets. Taking means and covariances of the model then gives:

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_g=\boldsymbol\alpha+\boldsymbol\beta\mu_{g,M},\qquad
\mathbf\Sigma_g=\sigma_{g,M}^2\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{\top}+\mathbf D_g.
$$

Substituting estimates from the same training observations gives:

$$
\hat{\mathbf g}_{\mathrm{SIM}}=\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}+\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}g_M^{\prime},\qquad
\hat{\mathbf\Sigma}_{g,\mathrm{SIM}}=s_{g,M}^2\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}^{\top}+\hat{\mathbf D}_g.
$$

The diagonal entries contain both market and residual variance, while the off-diagonal entries contain only the shared market contribution. Positive residual variances make the fitted covariance positive definite. These inputs replace the empirical ones in L6a's allocation problem.

**Which input changes when we use the SIM?** Only the covariance. With an intercept and the same training days, $\hat\alpha_i=g_i^{\prime}-\hat\beta_i g_M^{\prime}$, so $\hat{\mathbf g}_{\mathrm{SIM}}=\mathbf g^{\prime}$ and the reward inputs agree. The covariance changes because the model removes residual co-movement.

For two different assets, the sample covariance splits exactly into a part the SIM keeps and a part it omits:

$$
\hat\Sigma_{g,ij}
=\underbrace{\hat\beta_i\hat\beta_j s_{g,M}^2}_{\text{SIM keeps}}
+\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\mathbf r_i,\mathbf r_j)}_{\text{SIM omits}},\qquad i\ne j.
$$

On the diagonal, the SIM divides residual sums of squares by $N-2$, whereas the sample residual covariance uses $N-1$. Thus, the SIM residual contribution is larger by the factor $(N-1)/(N-2)$, which is nearly one with thousands of observations.

**Build a two-asset covariance.** Suppose the fitted betas are $(1,1.5)$, the market growth variance is $4\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$, and fitted residual variances are $(1,4)\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$. Then:

$$
\hat{\mathbf\Sigma}_{g,\mathrm{SIM}}
=4\begin{bmatrix}1&1.5\\1.5&2.25\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}5&6\\6&13\end{bmatrix}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}.
$$

For fixed weights, the portfolio beta is $\beta_p=\mathbf w^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$. Multiplying the covariance by the weight vector on both sides gives the general risk decomposition:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(g_p)=\beta_p^2\sigma_{g,M}^2+\sum_i w_i^2\sigma_{g,\varepsilon,i}^2.
$$

At equal weights, the fitted portfolio beta is $0.5(1)+0.5(1.5)=1.25$. Substituting the fitted inputs gives:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{SIM}}(g_p)
=\underbrace{1.25^2(4)}_{6.25\text{ market}}
+\underbrace{0.5^2(1)+0.5^2(4)}_{1.25\text{ residual}}
=7.5\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}.
$$

If the residual covariance were instead $1\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$, with the same diagonal entries, it would add the cross term $2(0.5)(0.5)(1)=0.5\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$ and the variance would be $8\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$. Positive residual co-movement increases the risk of these positive-weight holdings.

**Which risk can diversification reduce?** Residual risk. With $\lvert\mathcal P\rvert$ equally weighted assets and uncorrelated residuals of common variance $v$, the residual risk is $v/\lvert\mathcal P\rvert$. More generally, if every residual variance is at most $\bar\sigma^2$, the residual risk is at most $\bar\sigma^2/\lvert\mathcal P\rvert$. Market risk remains $\beta_p^2\sigma_{g,M}^2$, determined by the portfolio beta.

**How do the portfolio examples compare allocations?** The risky-assets example scores both weight vectors, the data-optimal weights and the SIM weights, under the sample covariance at common growth floors, then tests both on 2025 prices. At the same floor, the data-optimal weights can have no more sample-covariance risk than the SIM weights. Scoring both under one covariance separates the effect of choosing different holdings from the effect of measuring risk differently.

**Check.** In the two-asset calculation, replace residual covariance $1$ by $-1\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$. **Answer:** with the same diagonal entries, the variance becomes $7\,\mathrm{yr}^{-2}$. The SIM now overstates this portfolio's risk by omitting a negative covariance.
articles.keywords: SIM residual covariance diagonal idiosyncratic market risk diversification beta

articles.title: What changes when we lend or borrow?
articles.answer: The risk-free fraction controls exposure to the risky portfolio. Lending reduces that exposure, and borrowing increases it. When the risky portfolio has positive excess mean growth, borrowing raises both expected growth and risk.
articles.body:
We combine a risky portfolio with an asset whose growth rate is known over the holding period. The weight on the risk-free asset determines whether we lend or borrow. Here we use the course's fixed-weight, linear growth-rate proxy; the buy-and-hold wealth calculation instead follows the actual holdings as their wealth fractions change.



**What happens when we lend or borrow?** Put fraction $w_f$ in the risk-free asset and fraction $1-w_f$ in a fixed risky portfolio. The risk-free asset's known growth contributes to the mean and adds no variance:

$$
\mathbb E[g_c]=g_f+(1-w_f)(\mathbb E[g_p]-g_f),\qquad
\sigma_{g,c}=|1-w_f|\sigma_{g,p}.
$$

For daily observations ($\Delta t=1/252$ yr), suppose $g_f=0.02\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, $\mathbb E[g_p]=0.08\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, and $\sigma_{g,p}=3.0\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. A 50% risk-free allocation gives mean growth $0.05$ and standard deviation $1.5\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Borrowing 50% of initial wealth means $w_f=-0.5$: mean growth becomes $0.11$ and the standard deviation $4.5\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Borrowing increases both the risky exposure and the uncertainty.

For $w_f\leq1$, eliminating the risky fraction gives the capital allocation line (CAL):

$$
\mathbb E[g_c]=g_f+\mathrm{SR}_p\,\sigma_{g,c}.
$$

Its slope is the risky portfolio's Sharpe ratio, $(0.08-0.02)/3=0.02$. Under independent-increment scaling, the annualized ratio is $\sqrt{252}(0.02)=0.3175$. Expressing daily growth in inverse years does not, by itself, annualize this ratio.

**Check.** For a target mean growth of $0.065\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, what risk-free fraction is needed? **Answer:** $1-w_f=(0.065-0.02)/(0.08-0.02)=0.75$, so $w_f=0.25$ and the standard deviation is $2.25\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.
articles.keywords: capital allocation line CAL risk free lending borrowing leverage Sharpe ratio

articles.title: Which weights describe the risky fund and the whole investment?
articles.answer: The normalized risky weights describe the composition of the risky fund. The complete-investment weights also specify how much wealth is lent or borrowed at the risk-free rate.
articles.body:
**Which weights describe the risky fund, and which describe the whole investment?** With 1,000 USD of initial wealth, risky weights of $(0.30,0.45)$ put 300 USD in the first firm and 450 USD in the second, and the remaining 250 USD is lent at the risk-free rate. The risky weights sum to $0.75$, so $w_f=0.25$ and the normalized risky-fund weights are $(0.4,0.6)$. If we instead borrowed 50% of initial wealth, the complete-portfolio risky weights would be $(0.6,0.9)$, with the same normalized mix.

**Which risky portfolio defines the steepest capital allocation line?** The tangent portfolio maximizes excess mean growth per unit standard deviation. When the covariance is positive definite, signed risky weights are allowed, and the GMV mean growth exceeds $g_f$, the lecture obtains:

$$
\mathbf w_{\mathcal T}=\frac{\mathbf\Sigma_g^{-1}\mathbf e}{\mathbf1^{\top}\mathbf\Sigma_g^{-1}\mathbf e},
\qquad \mathbf e=\boldsymbol\mu_g-g_f\mathbf1.
$$

The inverse covariance adjusts the excess-growth vector for risk; the denominator makes the risky fund's weights sum to one. Long-only restrictions require a numerical solve. The lecture's problem (SIM-2) measures the risky weights as fractions of total initial wealth:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\underset{\mathbf w}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad
&\mathbf w^{\top}\hat{\mathbf\Sigma}_{g,\mathrm{SIM}}\mathbf w\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&(\hat{\mathbf g}_{\mathrm{SIM}}-g_f\mathbf1)^{\top}\mathbf w\geq g_\star-g_f,\\
&0\leq w_i\leq1,\qquad w_f=1-\mathbf1^{\top}\mathbf w.
\end{aligned}
$$

The risky weights can sum to more than one because borrowing is allowed. The bounds $w_i\leq1$ cap each risky position at the initial wealth, so they eventually limit how far we can borrow along a fixed risky mix.

**Recover the risky fund.** For feasible targets $g_\star>g_f$, and until an upper bound binds, we normalize a nonzero solution by its risky fraction. Every such target selects the same long-only tangent mix:

$$
\mathbf w_{\mathcal T}=\frac{\mathbf w}{\mathbf1^{\top}\mathbf w},\qquad
\mathbf w(g_\star)=(1-w_f)\mathbf w_{\mathcal T},\qquad
1-w_f=\frac{g_\star-g_f}{\hat{\mathbf g}_{\mathrm{SIM}}^{\top}\mathbf w_{\mathcal T}-g_f}.
$$

**Follow the complete investment.** The risky/risk-free example fixes the initial share counts and lets the risk-free position accumulate. With the tangent weights normalized to sum to one, wealth is:

$$
W_t=W_0\left[w_fe^{g_ft}+(1-w_f)\sum_i w_{\mathcal T,i}\frac{S_i(t)}{S_i(0)}\right].
$$

When $w_f<0$, the first term is a debt that grows over time. The example assumes one rate for both borrowing and lending. Under buy-and-hold, the risk-free and firm fractions drift, so the realized growth and risk need not equal the fixed-weight CAL predictions. The comparison uses 2025 prices that were held out of estimation and scores both tangent funds under the same sample covariance.

**Check.** Let $W_0=1{,}000$ USD, $w_f=-0.5$, $g_f=0.02\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, and suppose the risky fund gains 10% over one year. What is net wealth? **Answer:** net wealth is $1{,}000[-0.5e^{0.02}+1.5(1.10)]=1{,}139.90$ USD. The 1,650 USD risky holding is partly offset by a 510.10 USD repayment obligation.
articles.keywords: tangent tangency normalized weights complete investment risk free Sharpe

articles.title: Why discount cash flows, and what does positive NPV mean?
articles.answer: Discounting expresses cash flows from different dates as values on one common date, so we can compare and add them. A positive NPV means that, at the stated benchmark rate, the present value of the future net cash flows exceeds the initial cost.
articles.body:
**Why is receiving 110 USD next year worth less than receiving it today?** Suppose our benchmark pays 5% with annual compounding. An investment of 100 USD today becomes 105 USD in one year. To find what a promised 110 USD is worth today, we reverse that calculation: $110/1.05=104.76$ USD. Discounting asks how much we would need to invest today, at the benchmark rate, to reach the future payment.




**How do the cash-flow symbols become a value?** At date $j$, we multiply each cash amount $c_{j,k}$ by its direction $\nu_{j,k}$ (positive for a receipt, negative for a payment) and add the results. We then discount that date's net cash flow to time zero:

$$
\bar c_j=\sum_{k=1}^{m_j}c_{j,k}\nu_{j,k},\qquad
\operatorname{NPV}_0=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\mathcal D_{j,0}^{-1}\bar c_j.
$$

The first sum combines the cash flows that occur on the same date. The second adds their present values across dates. Paying 100 USD today and receiving 110 USD in one year therefore gives $\operatorname{NPV}_0=-100+110/1.05\approx4.76$ USD. The positive result means that the future payment beats the benchmark requirement by 4.76 USD in today's money. The discount factor is dimensionless, so each term in the NPV retains units of USD.

**What if there are two cash flows on the sale date?** Receiving 110 USD and paying a 2 USD fee gives $\bar c_1=110(+1)+2(-1)=108$ USD. We discount the net amount: $-100+108/1.05=2.86$ USD. This shows the role of each sum: the inner sum nets the cash flows on one date, and the outer sum discounts each date's net amount.

**Check.** Keep the 110 USD receipt, with no fee, but raise the benchmark to 10%. What is the NPV? **Answer:** NPV becomes $-100+110/1.10=0$. The cash gain is still 10 USD, but it now only matches the benchmark. When future receipts are uncertain, this calculation values only the cash-flow scenario we supply.
articles.keywords: discount present value NPV cash flow compounding benchmark

articles.title: How do coupon payments and yield determine a bond price?
articles.answer: The coupon rate sets the size of the promised coupon payments. The yield discounts those payments and par to the present. The payment schedule and the yield therefore play different roles.
articles.body:
**Where does the investment gain come from?** A bill held to maturity makes a single payment, par, and in the example below we buy it for less than par. A coupon bond also pays cash along the way. In both cases, we first identify the dated payments, then use the stated rate convention to connect them to today's price.




**From a bill quote to investment growth.** The bank-discount quote expresses the discount as a fraction of par. We first calculate the purchase price, then use the ratio of par to the purchase price to calculate the growth rate over the holding period:

$$
V_B=V_P\left(1-d\frac{D}{360}\right),\qquad
g_B=\frac{1}{T}\ln\left(\frac{V_P}{V_B}\right).
$$

For $V_P=100$ USD, $d=0.04$, and $D=90$ days, the bill costs 99 USD. If we measure the holding period as $T=90/365$ years, $g_B\approx0.04076\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. The quote is based on par and a 360-day year; the growth calculation is based on the amount invested and the holding-time convention we chose.

**What changes for a coupon bond?** We receive coupons along the way as well as par at maturity. Just after a coupon payment, and with a constant discount yield, the bond's value is the sum of the remaining discounted payments:

$$
V_B=\underbrace{V_P\mathcal D_{N,0}^{-1}}_{\text{present value of par}}
+\underbrace{C\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathcal D_{j,0}^{-1}}_{\text{present value of coupons}}.
$$

Each discount factor applies to the date of its payment. This is the L1b cash-flow calculation applied to the bond's payment schedule.

**Price a short coupon schedule.** Let par be 100 USD and the annual coupon rate be 4%, paid twice per year. Each coupon is $C=(0.04/2)(100)=2$ USD. With one year remaining, the payments are 2 USD in six months and 102 USD in one year. At a 6% nominal yield compounded semiannually:

$$
V_B=\frac{2}{1.03}+\frac{102}{1.03^2}=98.09\ \mathrm{USD}.
$$

The coupon rate fixes the promised 2 USD payments, and the yield discounts them. Here the coupon rate is below the yield, so the price is below par.

**Check.** Keep the same payments but use a 4% yield. What is the price? **Answer:** $2/1.02+102/1.02^2=100$ USD. The payments are unchanged, but their present values are larger.
articles.keywords: Treasury bond bill coupon yield par price discount security

articles.title: Why does a higher yield lower a bond’s price?
articles.answer: With the promised payments fixed, a higher yield discounts every payment more heavily, so the price falls. Duration and convexity summarize how sensitive the price is to small yield changes.
articles.body:
**Why does a higher yield lower a bond's price?** The promised payments are fixed. Raising the yield increases the denominator that discounts each payment, so every present value falls. For example, the two payments from L2a, 2 USD in six months and 102 USD in one year, are worth 100 USD at a 4% nominal yield and 98.09 USD at 6%. An investor who requires more growth from the same cash payments must pay a lower price to get it.




**What does duration measure?** At the 4% yield, the present values of the two payments are $2/1.02=1.9608$ and $102/1.02^2=98.0392$ USD. Dividing each by the 100 USD price gives its weight. Macaulay duration averages the payment times using these weights:

$$
D_{\mathrm{mac}}=0.5(0.019608)+1(0.980392)=0.9902\ \mathrm{yr}.
$$

Most of the value arrives on the last date, so the duration is close to one year. Shifting more present value to the earlier coupon would lower this weighted average time.

**How much will a yield change move the price?** Modified duration gives the first-order price sensitivity; convexity corrects for curvature. With the lecture's nominal-yield convention:

$$
D_{\mathrm{mod}}=\frac{D_{\mathrm{mac}}}{1+y/n},\qquad
\frac{\Delta V_B}{V_B}\approx-D_{\mathrm{mod}}\Delta y+\frac12K(\Delta y)^2.
$$

For a different bond with $D_{\mathrm{mod}}=5$ yr, $K=30\,\mathrm{yr}^2$, and a yield increase $\Delta y=0.01\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, the estimated relative price change is $-0.05+0.0015=-0.0485$, or a 4.85% decrease. This local approximation is most useful for small yield changes.

**How do we value payments with a yield curve?** The curve supplies a discount factor $D(0,t_j)$ for each payment date. Adding the discounted payments gives the price; setting that price equal to par and solving for the coupon rate gives:

$$
V_B=\sum_{j=1}^{N}X_jD(0,t_j),\qquad
c_{\mathrm{par}}=n\frac{1-D(0,t_N)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}D(0,t_j)}.
$$

The par coupon makes the present value of the coupons equal to the difference between par and the present value of the final par repayment.

For example, if the six-month and one-year discount factors are 0.98 and 0.95, the same two payments are worth $2(0.98)+102(0.95)=98.86$ USD. A par coupon must make up the $100-100(0.95)=5$ USD gap between par and the present value of the par repayment, so each coupon is $5/(0.98+0.95)=2.5907$ USD, corresponding to $c_{\mathrm{par}}=2(2.5907)/100=0.05181\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.

**Check.** In the duration-convexity example, lower the yield by 0.01 instead. What changes? **Answer:** the estimated change is $+0.05+0.0015=+5.15\%$. The duration term changes sign; the positive curvature correction does not.
articles.keywords: bond duration convexity yield curve spot par coupon sensitivity

| $\mathcal T$, $\mathbf w_{\mathcal T}$ | Tangent portfolio, which maximizes the Sharpe ratio, and its weights, which sum to one. | Label; 1 |
| $\sigma$ (tangent derivation) | Shorthand for $\sqrt{\mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf\Sigma_g\mathbf w}$ in T-2. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $c>0$ | Positive scale factor applied to the weights in the tangent and SIM-3 arguments. | 1 |
| $\mathbf w(g_\star)$ | SIM-2 risky weights for target $g_\star$, equal to $(1-w_f)\,\mathbf w_{\mathcal T}$ until a bound $w_i\leq1$ binds. | 1 |

notation.title: L7b: Utility and Risk Aversion
notation.markdown:
| Symbol | Meaning and context | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathcal X$, $x_i$ | Set of alternatives, such as bundles of goods, portfolios, or states of the world, and one alternative. | Context dependent |
| $U$ | Utility function, which assigns each alternative a number that ranks preferences. | utils |
| $x_i\succ x_j$, $x_i\sim x_j$ | The agent strictly prefers $x_i$ to $x_j$, or is indifferent between them. | Preference relations |
| $\mathbf x$, $\alpha_i$, $\beta$ | Bundle of goods, positive parameters of the standard utility forms, and the offset in the logarithmic utility. | Goods; form-specific |
| $\eta$ | CES elasticity of substitution: linear as $\eta\to\infty$, Cobb–Douglas as $\eta\to1$, and Leontief as $\eta\to0$. | 1 |
| $W$, $\mathbb E[U(W)]$ | Uncertain wealth outcome and its expected utility. | USD; utils |
| $\mathrm{CE}$, $\mathrm{RP}$ | Certainty equivalent, with $U(\mathrm{CE})=\mathbb E[U(W)]$, and risk premium $\mathbb E(W)-\mathrm{CE}$. | USD |
| $w$ (Arrow–Pratt) | Wealth level at which the risk-aversion measures are evaluated. | USD |
| $r(w)$, $\bar r(w)$ | Arrow–Pratt absolute risk aversion $-U''(w)/U'(w)$ and relative risk aversion $w\,r(w)$. | $\mathrm{USD}^{-1}$; 1 |
| $a$, $b$, $\tau$ | Coefficients of the linear utility of wealth and the exponent of the power utility. | utils/USD; utils; 1 |

notation.title: L7b: Mean-Variance Utility on the Capital Allocation Line
notation.markdown:
| Symbol | Meaning and context | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $g_f$, $w_f$, $c$, $\mathcal T$ | Risk-free growth rate, risk-free fraction, complete portfolio, and tangent portfolio, as in L7a. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$; 1; labels |
| $A$ | Risk-aversion coefficient, which plays the role of $\bar r$. A larger $A$ charges more for the same risk. | 1 |
| $U(w_f)$ | Mean-variance utility of the complete portfolio: $\mathbb E[g_c]-\tfrac{A}{2}\,\Delta t\,\sigma_{g,c}^2$. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $\Delta t\,\sigma_{g,c}^2$ | Squared volatility of the complete portfolio, on the scale of the GBM volatility. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $\mathbb E[g_{\mathcal T}]$, $\sigma_{g,\mathcal T}$ | Expected growth rate and growth-rate standard deviation of the tangent portfolio. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $w_f^\star$ | Risk-free fraction that maximizes mean-variance utility. | 1 |
| $A_{\mathcal T}$ | Risk aversion of the investor who holds $\mathcal T$ alone. Investors with a larger $A$ lend, and investors with a smaller $A$ borrow. | 1 |
| $\delta$, $\delta^\star$ | Income cut of the risky job in the income-gamble interview, as a fraction of the sure income. At $\delta^\star$ a person cannot choose between the two jobs, and this cut fixes $\bar r$. | 1 |

notation.title: L7b: Utility over Holdings
notation.markdown:
| Symbol | Meaning and context | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $S_i(t)$ | Price of asset $i$ at decision time $t$. | USD/share |
| $W_{\mathcal P}(t)$ | Wealth to allocate over the assets in $\mathcal P$ at time $t$. | USD |
| $n_i$, $n_i^\star$ | Share count of asset $i$ and its optimal value. | Shares |
| $n_{\min}$ | Floor on every share count, which keeps the utility finite when $\gamma_i<0$. | Shares |
| $\gamma_i$ | Preference weight: the Cobb–Douglas exponent of asset $i$, in $(-1,1)$. | 1 |
| $\mathcal A^{+}$, $\mathcal A^{-}$ | Preferred set $\{i:\gamma_i>0\}$, the basket, and non-preferred set $\{i:\gamma_i\leq0\}$. | Index sets |
| $W_{\mathrm{adj}}$ | Budget left for $\mathcal A^{+}$ after buying the floors: $W_{\mathcal P}(t)-n_{\min}\sum_{k\in\mathcal A^{-}}S_k(t)$. | USD |
| $\mathcal L$, $\lambda$ | Lagrangian and budget multiplier in the Cobb–Douglas derivation. | 1; $\mathrm{USD}^{-1}$ |
| $U_{\mathrm{CES}}$ | CES holding utility over the preferred set, with elasticity $\eta$. | utils |
| $\gamma_i/S_i(t)$ | Bang for the buck: preference weight per dollar of share price. | Shares/USD |

notation.title: L7b: Preference Weights from the Single Index Model
notation.markdown:
| Symbol | Meaning and context | Units |
|---|---|---|
| $\gamma_i(t)$ | Preference weight of asset $i$ on day $t$: $\tanh\bigl(h\,[\alpha_i/\beta_i^{\xi_t}+\beta_i^{1-\xi_t}\tilde g_{M,t}]\bigr)$. | 1 |
| $h$ | Horizon that makes the argument of the preference model dimensionless, $h=1$ year. | yr |
| $\alpha_i$, $\beta_i$ | L6b SIM intercept and beta. The model assumes $\beta_i>0$. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$; 1 |
| $\tilde g_{M,t}$ | Recent market growth rate: the 252-day EMA of daily SPY growth rates. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $\xi_t$ | Market-state signal: positive (bearish) after a falling market and negative (bullish) after a rising one. | 1 |
| $g_{M,t}$ | Daily market growth rate $\ln(S_t/S_{t-1})/\Delta t$. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |
| $S_t$, $\bar S_t$ | SPY share price and its EMA. | USD/share |
| $L$, $\omega$ | EMA window in trading days and weight on the newest price, $\omega=2/(L+1)$. L5a's decay factor $\lambda$ corresponds to $1-\omega$. | Days; 1 |
| $L_{\mathrm{short}}$, $L_{\mathrm{long}}$, $L_{\mathrm{growth}}$ | EMA windows of 21, 63, and 252 trading days. | Days |
| $\bar S_t^{\mathrm{short}}$, $\bar S_t^{\mathrm{long}}$ | Short and long price EMAs, whose crossover sets $\xi_t$. | USD/share |
| $G$ | Gain chosen on the training data so that $\lvert\xi_t\rvert\leq1$ on 99% of training days. | 1 |
| $-\alpha_i/\beta_i$ | Basket threshold: asset $i$ enters when $\tilde g_{M,t}$ exceeds it. | $\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ |

notation.title: Symbols Whose Meaning Changes with Context
notation.markdown:
| Symbol | Contexts to distinguish | Where |
|---|---|---|
| $\alpha$ | Tail index; regression significance level; Dirichlet concentration; SIM intercept; parameter of a standard utility form. | L3a; L4b; L5b-L6a; L6b-L7b; L7b |
| $\beta$ | SIM beta (market exposure); offset in the logarithmic utility. | L6b-L7b; L7b |
| $\gamma$ | Factor sensitivity $\gamma_{ij}$; Cobb–Douglas preference weight $\gamma_i$. | L6b; L7b |
| $\delta$ | Option sensitivity in the orientation preview; growth innovation $\delta_k$ in EMA; income cut in the income-gamble interview. | L1a; L5a; L7b |
| $\lambda$ | EMA decay factor; GMV equality-constraint multiplier; Cobb–Douglas budget multiplier. | L5a; L6a; L7b |
| $\mu$, $\mu_g$ | Drift of expected share price; mean log growth. Under GBM, $\mu_g=\mu-\sigma^2/2$. | L4b-L5b |
| $\sigma_g$, $\sigma$ | Standard deviation of observed growth rates; diffusion volatility. They satisfy $\sigma=\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\sigma_g$ under the matched GBM convention. In the L7a tangent derivation, $\sigma$ abbreviates the portfolio growth-rate standard deviation. | L3a-L7b; L7a |
| $C$, $\mathbf C$ | Cash coupon; covariance-rate matrix. Boldface and context distinguish them. | L2a; L5b |
| $\mathbf\Sigma_g$, $\mathbf C$ | Growth covariance; covariance rate, with $\mathbf C=\Delta t\,\mathbf\Sigma_g$. | L5b-L6b |
| $D$, $D(0,t)$, $D_{\mathrm{mod}}$, $D_{\mathrm{mac}}$, $\mathbf D_g$ | Days to bill maturity; discount factor; duration measures; observed down-multiplier set; diagonal residual covariance. | L2a; L2b; L3b; L6b |
| $n$ | Compounding periods per year; tail-analysis sample size; simulated path count; share count $n_i$. | L1b-L2a; L3a; L6a |
| $d$ | Bill discount quote; lattice down factor; frontier coefficient $ac-b^2$. | L2a; L3b; L6a |
| $K$, $K_N$ | Bond convexity; terminal price target; binomial up-count $K_N$; bootstrap dataset count. | L2b; L5a; L4a; L6b |
| $R$, $R^2$ | Solver growth floor $R=g_\star$; coefficient of determination $R^2$. | L6a-L6b |
| $M$ | Growth-magnitude bound; Monte Carlo path count; asset count; market subscript. | L3b; L4b; L5b; L6b-L7b |
| $T$, $t$ | L3a uses $T$ for a count of prices; lattice $t$ is a step count; continuous-time models use time in years. | L3a-L6b |
| $p$ | Up probability; number of regression parameters; risky-portfolio label. | L3b; L4b; L6b-L7a |
| $\rho(k)$, $\rho_T$, $\rho_{ij}$ | Autocorrelation; scaled NPV (including L4a node function $\rho(k)$); cross-asset correlation. | L3a; L4a; L5b |
| $W(t)$, $W_t$ | Wiener process; portfolio wealth, including $W_{\mathcal P}(t)$; uncertain wealth outcome $W$ in expected utility. | L4b; L5b-L7b; L7b |
| $w$, $w_i$, $w_f$ | Wealth level in the Arrow–Pratt measures; portfolio weight; risk-free fraction. | L7b; L5b-L7b; L6b-L7b |
| $\mathbf\Sigma$, $\mathbf\Sigma_g$ | Diagonal singular-value matrix in SVD; growth covariance matrix. | L6b |
| $r_{i,t}$, $\mathbf r_i$, $r(w)$ | Interval log return $r_{i,t}=g_{i,t}\Delta t$; fitted regression residual vector; absolute risk aversion, with relative risk aversion $\bar r(w)$. | L6b; L4b/L6b; L7b |
| $\hat{\mathbf X}$ | Design matrix with time as predictor; design matrix with market growth as predictor. | L4b; L6b |
| $\tau$ | Lattice lag; real-valued up-count threshold; reference year for annualizing a Sharpe ratio; power-utility exponent. | L3b; L4a; L6b-L7a; L7b |
| $\nu$, $\nu_{j,k}$ | Student-$t$ degrees of freedom; regression residual degrees of freedom; cash-flow direction. | L3a; L4b; L1b |
| $X$, $X_j$, $\mathbf X_t$, $\mathbf X$ | Growth magnitude; bond cash flow or lattice up indicator; branch-count vector; worked-example noise vector. | L3a; L2b/L3b; L4a; L5b |
| $c$, $c_{j,k}$ | Coupon rate; frontier coefficient; complete-portfolio subscript; cash-flow amount; positive scale factor on the weights. | L2a-L2b; L6a; L6b-L7b; L1b; L7a |
| $A$, $\mathbf A$ | Risk-aversion coefficient in mean-variance utility; MAGBM loading matrix with $\mathbf A\mathbf A^{\top}=\mathbf C$. | L7b; L5b-L6a |
| $G$, $\mathbf G$ | Gain of the market-state signal; growth data matrix. | L7b; L5b-L6a |
| $L(x)$, $L_t$, $L$ | Slowly varying tail factor; number of lattice count states; EMA window in trading days. | L3a; L4a; L7b |
